public_rationale: Measurement research distinguishes acquired task skill from the capacity to generalize. Experiments also show substantially stronger performance on one formulation than on a closely related transfer task. These findings support the limited claim that impressive task performance alone is insufficient. They do not establish that current systems lack all generalization, or that behavioral testing cannot establish general intelligence.
limitations: The empirical example concerns particular systems and tasks, not every model available in February 2026.
The identified transfer failure can be mitigated.
The conclusion applies to task performance alone, not to every possible collection of controlled evaluations.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Impressive task-level performance is not sufficient evidence of general intelligence.

statement.excerpt: Task-level performance, even when impressive, is not sufficient evidence of general intelligence.
statement.document_title: Rumors of AGI’s arrival have been greatly exaggerated

from_speaker: is not sufficient evidence of general intelligence
our_interpretation: The ordinary reading is that high performance on individual fixed tasks alone does not establish flexible transfer across broad unfamiliar tasks.
This does not say task performance is irrelevant, or that sufficiently broad and well-controlled behavioral evaluations cannot provide evidence of intelligence.
Treat this as a claim about the evidentiary relationship illustrated by research available through publication, rather than a claim restricted to one current model.
criteria.support_condition: Measurement research or controlled experiments show that strong performance on tested tasks can coexist with failure to transfer the relevant knowledge or skill.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Task scores alone reliably establish the specified broad generalization, without additional assumptions, controls, or transfer evaluations.

evidence.excerpt: High skill is not high intelligence
evidence.locator: Section II.2.1, summary of the proposed intelligence measure
evidence.explanation: The paper explains how prior knowledge and training can produce task skill without establishing the ability to acquire new skills. This supports the ordinary distinction in the claim, within an explicitly stated measurement framework.

Accuracy drops substantially when the direction of a factual relationship is reversed. Together with the paper's controlled training experiments, this demonstrates why success on one task does not establish even closely related transfer.

Training that induces suitable relational representations improves transfer. This limits any inference that language models inherently cannot generalize, but does not make task performance alone sufficient evidence of general intelligence.
